chapter_theme: Reading desire that won't declare itself. The lovers communicate through lowered eyes, half-smiles and feigned indifference, until spoken words are declared useless.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar assigns the signs to the man (1091-1095), his inference from a rebuff by the friend (1096-1097), his relief at her smile (1098), and the friend's own inference about the couple (1099-1100).

1091.reading: The man sees two looks in her kohl-lined eyes: one gives him the sickness and the other is its cure.

positions.position: The painful look discloses desire in her mind and the healing look shows her love; he rejects calling the first a neutral look, since one-sided pain wouldn't be mutual love.
positions.quote: நோய் செய்யும் நோக்கு அவள் மனத்தனாய காமக்குறிப்பினை வெளிப்படுத்துகின்ற நோக்கு.

positions.position: The two looks are successive: the first look that hurt him, then a later one mixed with shyness and concern for his pain.

1092.reading: The man says the brief look her eyes steal is not half of love's fulfilment but more than half.
1092.nuance: The arithmetic is odd until you see why it works. Parimelazhagar says the glance guarantees that union will follow, so its value lies in what it promises. Stealing also suits the setting: this is secret love, and the eyes are the first thieves.

1093.reading: The man says she looked, and having looked lowered her head, and that gesture was water poured into the bond between them.
1093.nuance: The verse says only யாப்பு, a binding, and water poured into it. The growing crop of love that makes the image cohere comes from the commentators, and Parimelazhagar notes that the metaphor is only partly stated. Lowering her head is what waters the bond, so modesty here works for desire and not against it.

1094.reading: The man observes that when he looks she looks at the ground, and when he doesn't she looks at him and smiles softly.
1094.nuance: The whole verse is timing. Their eyes never meet, and that very avoidance tells him she is watching. Parimelazhagar takes மெல்ல நகும் as rejoicing inwardly without showing it, and mentions that others read it as a visible smile.

1095.reading: The man says that she doesn't look at him directly, but smiles as though narrowing one eye.

positions.position: She narrows one eye as she glances; the 'as though' is there because even this isn't openly done.
He reads the line as 'at one moment', and the verb as agreeing: she smiles as one who has consented.

1096.reading: The man reflects that the words of those without real anger are quickly seen through, even when they speak like strangers.

positions.position: The harsh speaker is the friend, who is sending him away while really seeking to help; he says this to himself.
positions.quote: தோழி சேண்படுத்தவழி அவள் குறிப்பு அறிந்த தலைமகன் தன்னுள்ளே சொல்லியது.

positions.position: The case is one where the body shows agreement and speech refuses, which is taken as consent.
The harsh speaker is the woman herself, hiding love under a stranger's manner.

1097.reading: The man reasons that small harsh words without anger and looks like an enemy's are the signs of those who are close while seeming distant.
1097.nuance: 1096 and 1097 give him a rule for treating refusal as disguise, and the verses rest it entirely on செறாஅ, the absence of real anger. In my reading that condition is doing all the work, and it is exactly what the man can't verify from outside. Parimelazhagar's conclusion is that he needn't fear such signs.

1098.reading: The man says that when he looks, she softens and smiles gently, and there is something special about the swaying woman at that moment.

positions.position: ஏர் here is the good sign that shows in her smile, a promise that won't fail him after his pleading look.
ஏர் is beauty, the quality that surpasses her form at that moment.

1099.reading: Looking at each other with a stranger's common glance is found only in lovers; Parimelazhagar gives this to the friend, who is working out the affair, while the other commentators name no speaker.
1099.nuance: A public pretence of indifference becomes the evidence. The couple's disguise gives them away to the one person placed to notice, so this is close observation from outside the romance.

1100.reading: Once eyes agree with eyes in their look, spoken words have no use at all; the speaker is the friend for Parimelazhagar and the man for Manakkudavar.
1100.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes the claim very concrete: the useless words are the couple's cover stories, hers about guarding the millet field and his about hunting. Out of context it reads as a maxim about wordless love.

positions.position: The friend, having heard both, speaks in general terms about what she has noticed.
positions.quote: இருவர் சொல்லும் கேட்டு உலகியல்மேல் வைத்துக் கூறியவாறு.

positions.position: The man, about to approach her, speaks to his own heart.

links.note: Both chapters are named குறிப்பறிதல. In 709, a skilled reader of eyes can tell enmity from friendship in a court. 1097 warns that a lover's eyes can put on enmity while friendly, so the statecraft skill has to work harder here.
In 1091 one look wounds and another heals. In 1102 the woman herself is both the disease and its medicine. The paradox grows from a glance to the whole person once they have united.

source_issues: 1098: Kalaignar's entry ends with stray text about a rhetorical figure (ஆகியவற்றைக் காணலாம். ஆ. அணி நலம் ...) that is editorial matter from another source, not commentary on this verse. It was not used.
1095: Manakkudavar's gloss implies a different reading, ஒருகால், where the verse has ஒருகண், and its நகா நின்தள் looks like a typo for நகாநின்றாள்.
